name: The Forgotten Hour

detectability.signature: Persistent chronometric drag signature — onboard clocks lose synchronization at a rate proportional to proximity, detectable as a smooth gradient in tachyon background radiation

proximity: Ship chronometers begin drifting, losing approximately one second per minute relative to external reference frames
Crew members report a pervasive sense of languor, as though thoughts require slightly more effort than usual
contact: Time dilation reaches a ratio of roughly 60:1 — one hour inside corresponds to sixty hours outside
Communication signals stretch into incomprehensibility, arriving as low-frequency drones that take hours to decode
Biological processes slow proportionally, though subjective experience remains normal for those affected
prolonged_exposure: Accumulated temporal debt becomes disorienting upon exit — crew members emerge to find weeks or months have passed
Psychological distress from temporal displacement, including identity dissociation and grief for lost time
Subtle cellular desynchronization as different organ systems readjust to normal time flow at different rates

age: Estimated 4.2 billion years — likely a remnant of a stellar collapse that folded local spacetime into a permanent dilation well
phenomena: Ships that enter and exit report seeing their own entry point as a frozen tableau — the vessel they were appears to hang motionless at the boundary
Light from distant stars bends and redshifts as it passes through the field, creating a visible halo of dimmed, reddened starlight
Radio transmissions from within the field arrive stretched and deepened, sometimes taking days to convey a message spoken in seconds
Debris that drifts into the field appears to stop moving, hanging in place for years before eventually completing its transit
hazards: Temporal displacement upon exit — a brief survey mission can result in the loss of months or years of external time
Navigation systems relying on external time signals fail within the field, requiring dead reckoning
Supply calculations based on subjective time become dangerously inaccurate relative to actual elapsed duration
opportunities: The stable dilation effect could be used for long-duration experiments that require patience — years of chemical processes completed in subjective days
Emergency medical applications: critically injured patients could be placed within the field to slow deterioration while rescue is organized
Theoretical physicists have proposed using the field boundary as a natural laboratory for studying the relationship between gravity and time
known_incidents: The survey vessel Quiet Meridian entered the field for what its crew experienced as a three-day mapping mission; upon exit, fourteen months had elapsed and their posting had been reassigned
A research buoy placed at the field's center in 2241 has transmitted a total of forty-seven minutes of data over the course of thirty-one external years
description: The Forgotten Hour is invisible. There is no shimmer, no distortion, no visible boundary to mark where normal time ends and dilated time begins. The only clue is the gradual reddening of background starlight as photons lose energy climbing out of the temporal gradient, and the slow, inexorable drift of every clock on board toward disagreement with the outside universe. The field is perfectly spherical, centered on a point in empty space where a massive star once collapsed under conditions that modern astrophysics cannot fully explain.

Within the field, time passes at a fraction of its normal rate. The effect is smooth and predictable — there are no sudden transitions, no turbulence, no chaotic fluctuations. A ship can enter, conduct its business, and leave without incident. The danger is not violent; it is arithmetic. Every hour spent inside costs days outside. Every day costs weeks. The field does not harm those within it. It simply steals their future, one dilated second at a time.

The anomaly was first cataloged in 2208 by the long-range survey program Cartographer's Burden, which noted that probe signals from the region arrived with inexplicable delays. Early expeditions confirmed the dilation effect and established its boundaries with high precision. The loss of the Quiet Meridian — not to destruction but to temporal displacement — prompted the establishment of mandatory temporal budgeting protocols for any vessel entering a known dilation field.

The Forgotten Hour remains a subject of quiet fascination among navigators and physicists alike. Its perfect stability makes it one of the most studied temporal anomalies in known space, and a small constellation of monitoring satellites maintains a perpetual watch on its boundary. Proposals to use the field for industrial or medical purposes surface periodically but face opposition from temporal ethicists who argue that deliberately displacing individuals in time raises profound moral questions. The field itself, of course, is indifferent to the debate. It simply waits, as it has for billions of years, turning hours into moments and moments into forgotten time.
